meta.title: How GPS Works: Time into Position

plan.title: How GPS Works: Time into Position
plan.hook: Your phone finds itself by listening for clocks. Each satellite announces when its signal left; the receiver turns that tiny travel time into a distance — and the arithmetic is so sensitive that a single microsecond of timing error becomes 300 metres of position error.
objectives: Convert a signal travel time into a range estimate, and a timing error into the range error it causes
Explain why a receiver solves for four unknowns — three coordinates and its own clock offset — and needs at least four satellites
Distinguish accuracy from repeatability and judge a fix by geometry and error sources rather than displayed digits

sections.heading: Tiny time errors become large distances
sections.body:
GPS satellites broadcast information that lets a receiver estimate satellite position and signal transmission time. Comparing transmit and receive times gives apparent travel time. Multiplying by signal speed turns that interval into a range estimate.

Radio signals travel at about 300 million metres per second. One microsecond therefore corresponds to roughly 300 metres.
sections.visual: A satellite transmits its send time. The receiver compares send and receive times, then multiplies the signal’s travel time by the speed of light. A one-microsecond timing error corresponds to about 300 metres of range error.

questions.q: How does a receiver turn a radio signal into a distance?
questions.hint: Two times are compared, and their difference is scaled by something.
questions.answer: It compares the signal's transmit time with its receive time to get an apparent travel time, then multiplies by the signal speed. That product is the range estimate.

questions.q: Why does a one-microsecond clock error matter so much?
questions.hint: Multiply one microsecond by the speed the signal travels.
questions.answer: Radio signals travel at about 300 million metres per second, so one microsecond corresponds to roughly 300 metres of range. Tiny time errors become large distances.

sections.heading: Three coordinates plus one clock
sections.body: Real receivers must estimate their own clock offset as well as location, so the standard unconstrained three-dimensional problem has four unknowns: three position coordinates and one clock offset. At least four suitably placed satellites are normally required.
sections.visual: Each satellite supplies a range sphere. A real GNSS receiver solves for x, y, z and its clock offset using at least four measurements; this sketch is a 2D analogy.

questions.q: Why are three satellites not enough for a full fix?
questions.hint: Count the unknowns the receiver itself brings to the problem.
questions.answer: The receiver must estimate its own clock offset as well as its position — four unknowns: three coordinates and one clock offset. At least four suitably placed satellites are normally required.

questions.q: What does each satellite contribute to the solution?
questions.hint: The visual describes a geometric shape per satellite.
questions.answer: A range: the receiver lies somewhere on a sphere of that radius around the satellite. Combining at least four such measurements pins down position and clock offset together.

sections.heading: More digits do not guarantee a better fix
sections.body: Accuracy means closeness to the true position. Repeatability describes how tightly repeated estimates cluster. Extra decimal places can simply decorate a noisy estimate.
sections.visual: Geometry, signal quality, clock and atmosphere all matter more than display resolution. Precision is not the same as accuracy.

questions.q: What is the difference between accuracy and repeatability?
questions.hint: One is about the true position; the other is about the estimates among themselves.
questions.answer: Accuracy is closeness to the true position. Repeatability describes how tightly repeated estimates cluster — a receiver can be repeatably wrong.

questions.q: A receiver shows eight decimal places. Should you trust the fix more?
questions.hint: The heading of this section is the warning label.
questions.answer: Not on that evidence. Extra decimal places can simply decorate a noisy estimate; geometry, signal quality, clock and atmosphere matter more than display resolution.

questions.q: A receiver's clock is off by 2 microseconds. Roughly how large a range error does that create?
choices: About 3 metres
About 60 metres
About 600 metres
About 6 kilometres
questions.explain: One microsecond at signal speed (about 300 million metres per second) corresponds to roughly 300 metres. Two microseconds double that to about 600 metres.

questions.q: A GPS range estimate is computed as…
choices: Signal travel time divided by signal speed
Signal travel time multiplied by signal speed
Transmit time minus satellite position
Signal speed divided by travel time
questions.explain: Comparing transmit and receive times gives the apparent travel time; multiplying by the signal speed turns that interval into a range estimate.

questions.q: The four unknowns in the standard GPS problem are…
choices: Three satellite positions and one clock offset
Three position coordinates and the receiver's clock offset
Four satellite clock offsets
Latitude, longitude, and two clock offsets
questions.explain: Real receivers must estimate their own clock offset as well as location: three position coordinates plus one clock offset — which is why at least four suitably placed satellites are normally required.

questions.q: Why does the receiver need to solve for its own clock offset at all?
choices: Because satellite clocks are unreliable
Because its range estimates are built from its own receive times, which its clock error corrupts
Because four unknowns make the maths easier
Because the satellites move during the signal's travel
questions.explain: Ranges come from comparing transmit times with the receiver's own receive times. Any error in the receiver's clock lands directly in every range, so the offset is estimated as part of the solution.

questions.q: A receiver reports the same wrong position, tightly clustered, on every reading. That is…
choices: High accuracy and high repeatability
Low accuracy but high repeatability
High accuracy but low repeatability
Neither accuracy nor repeatability
questions.explain: Repeatability describes how tightly repeated estimates cluster — they cluster tightly here. Accuracy is closeness to the true position, and the position is wrong, so accuracy is low.

questions.q: Which evidence best supports trusting a GPS fix?
choices: The display shows many decimal places
The reading updates quickly
Good satellite geometry and clean signals with understood error sources
The receiver is an expensive model
questions.explain: The section lists what matters: geometry, signal quality, clock and atmosphere. Reported precision is not true accuracy — extra digits can decorate a noisy estimate.

sections.title: A time measurement becomes a range
bullets: Satellites broadcast position information and transmission time.
Travel time × signal speed = range estimate.
Signals move at about 300 million m/s.
A 1 μs timing error is roughly 300 m of range error.
sections.notes: GPS is a timing system wearing a map's clothes. The receiver never measures distance directly — it measures how long the signal took and multiplies by the speed of light. That multiplication is why tiny clock errors explode into hundreds of metres.
sections.visual: A satellite transmits its send time. The receiver compares send and receive times, then multiplies the signal’s travel time by the speed of light. A one-microsecond timing error corresponds to about 300 metres of range error.

sections.title: Three coordinates plus one clock
bullets: The receiver solves for x, y, z — and its own clock offset.
Four unknowns need at least four suitably placed satellites.
Each satellite supplies a range sphere.
sections.notes: The receiver's clock is cheap and wrong, so the solution treats that error as a fourth unknown instead of pretending it away. Four satellites give the four measurements the problem needs.
sections.visual: Each satellite supplies a range sphere. A real GNSS receiver solves for x, y, z and its clock offset using at least four measurements; this sketch is a 2D analogy.

sections.title: Precision is not accuracy
bullets: Accuracy: closeness to the true position.
Repeatability: how tightly repeated estimates cluster.
Extra decimal places can decorate a noisy estimate.
Trust geometry, signal quality, clock and atmosphere — not digit count.
sections.notes: A long decimal readout feels rigorous but says nothing about truth. A fix deserves trust when the satellites are well spread and the error sources are understood.
sections.visual: Geometry, signal quality, clock and atmosphere all matter more than display resolution. Precision is not the same as accuracy.

enrichment.audioTitle: How GPS Works: Time into Position — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: A satellite's signal left at a known time and arrives a fraction of a second later. What does the receiver actually compute from that?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: The travel time — receive time minus transmit time — then multiply by the signal speed to get a range.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Right. Now the punchline: the signal travels at about 300 million metres per second. Your clock is off by one microsecond. How wrong is the range?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: One microsecond times that speed... about 300 metres. That is brutal.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: It is. Which raises the next problem: the receiver's clock is exactly the kind of clock that drifts. What does the solution do about it?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Use more satellites until the clock error cancels?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Nearly — it promotes the clock offset to an unknown and solves for it. How many unknowns does that make, in three dimensions?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Three coordinates plus the clock offset: four. So at least four satellites, each giving a range sphere.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly — suitably placed ones. Last topic: your receiver shows a position with eight decimal places and it barely changes between readings. Impressed?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Careful. Repeatability is the tight clustering. Accuracy is closeness to the true position. What can those extra digits be doing?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Decorating a noisy estimate. The clustering could be tightly wrong.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: So what earns your trust instead of the digit count?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Satellite geometry, signal quality, and the clock and atmosphere error sources — the things the section lists.
